turns_text: [SEG0001] person_1 (NURSE): Come through, love, I'll grab your obs before the doctor. Hop on the scales.
[SEG0002] person_1 (NURSE): Ninety-seven kilos. Blood pressure one thirty-eight over eighty-four, pulse seventy-two. Sitting, and quite steady.
[SEG0003] person_1 (NURSE): Any medicine allergies I should put on the file?
[SEG0004] person_2 (PATIENT): No.
[SEG0005] person_3 (DOCTOR): G'day. I'm Dr Shah. Good you've got your daughter with you. What's brought you in?
[SEG0006] person_2 (PATIENT): Knee.
[SEG0007] person_3 (DOCTOR): Which knee, and what sets it off? Stairs are often the giveaway with this sort of pain, so I'm listening for that.
[SEG0008] person_2 (PATIENT): Right. Stairs.
[SEG0009] person_4 (FAMILY_MEMBER): It's the right knee. Going down the stairs sets it off, coming up is fine, and it wakes him at night.
[SEG0010] person_3 (DOCTOR): How long's it been like that?
[SEG0011] person_2 (PATIENT): Years.
[SEG0012] person_4 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Not years, Dad. Since August, after the trip. Eight months.
[SEG0013] person_3 (DOCTOR): I'll leave the timing loose, about eight months to a few years. Better a range than a date we made up.
[SEG0014] person_3 (DOCTOR): How bad is it? And I'm wondering about swelling, and about stiffness in the morning.
[SEG0015] person_2 (PATIENT): Bad.
[SEG0016] person_3 (DOCTOR): Swelling, though?
[SEG0017] person_2 (PATIENT): Mm, I suppose.
[SEG0018] person_3 (DOCTOR): Morning stiffness?
[SEG0019] person_2 (PATIENT): Sometimes. Not really.
[SEG0020] person_3 (DOCTOR): I'll treat both of those as maybes, not facts. Does the knee lock, or give way?
[SEG0021] person_2 (PATIENT): No.
[SEG0022] person_3 (DOCTOR): What are you using on it? Gel, tablets from the chemist?
[SEG0023] person_2 (PATIENT): Gel.
[SEG0024] person_4 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Voltaren gel. He's meant to put it on the knee twice a day, but he skips the morning most days. Nagging hasn't fixed it.
[SEG0025] person_3 (DOCTOR): Diclofenac gel, twice a day on paper, and I'm not sure it actually happens. Tablets as well, from the chemist?
[SEG0026] person_2 (PATIENT): Sometimes.
[SEG0027] person_3 (DOCTOR): Which tablets, what strength?
[SEG0028] person_2 (PATIENT): Voltaren. Twenty-five. Think.
[SEG0029] person_4 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Those are the fifty milligram Voltaren, Dad. One when the pain's really bad, not every day.
[SEG0030] person_3 (DOCTOR): Strength's not agreed, twenty-five or fifty, so I won't write a dose. By mouth, only on the bad days. Any stomach problems with them? Reflux, ulcers?
[SEG0031] person_2 (PATIENT): No.
[SEG0032] person_3 (DOCTOR): Before that, were you on a script anti-inflammatory?
[SEG0033] person_4 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Naproxen. Two hundred and fifty milligrams twice a day, for the knee, from his old GP.
[SEG0034] person_3 (DOCTOR): Still taking the naproxen?
[SEG0035] person_2 (PATIENT): Stopped. March.
[SEG0036] person_3 (DOCTOR): Stopped in March. That's discontinued, not something you're on now. Did you ever actually start the glucosamine the chemist suggested?
[SEG0037] person_2 (PATIENT): No.
[SEG0038] person_3 (DOCTOR): Never started, so it stays off the list. And you're still on the amlodipine?
[SEG0039] person_2 (PATIENT): Yeah.

[SEG0040] person_4 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Side note while I remember. I take biotin for my hair, that's mine, not his. Mum, his wife, has diabetes and she's on metformin, five hundred milligrams twice a day. His amlodipine is five milligrams every morning for the blood pressure, ongoing for years, and he lives with me and Mum, retired last year.

[SEG0041] person_3 (DOCTOR): Your biotin and your mother's metformin do not go on his chart. Her diabetes I'll record as his wife's history. Hypertension ongoing, amlodipine five milligrams by mouth every morning. Now the knee itself.
[SEG0042] person_3 (DOCTOR): Right knee. Tender along the medial joint line, crepitus when you bend, flexion a bit short of full, and no effusion that I can feel.

[SEG0043] person_3 (DOCTOR): Working impression is osteoarthritis of that knee. Going down stairs is mechanical and it fits. Night waking means I can't fully rule out an inflammatory flare, so that stays a possibility, not a firm label.
[SEG0044] person_3 (DOCTOR): Weight's ninety-seven kilos, and that's a lot of load through a sore knee. Easing off a few kilos would help the joint. Mechanics, not a lecture.
[SEG0045] person_4 (FAMILY_MEMBER): He gets heartburn, you know. He said no stomach problems.
[SEG0046] person_2 (PATIENT): Heartburn. After tablets.
[SEG0047] person_3 (DOCTOR): Right, so there is heartburn, and it comes after the diclofenac tablets. The earlier no doesn't hold. When did the heartburn start?
[SEG0048] person_2 (PATIENT): Dunno.
[SEG0049] person_3 (DOCTOR): No date, then. Any chest pain with it, pain into the arm, or shortness of breath?
[SEG0050] person_2 (PATIENT): No.

[SEG0051] person_3 (DOCTOR): No chest pain and no breathlessness, which is reassuring. I'd like you to ease off those Voltaren tablets because of the heartburn, keep the gel if your skin tolerates it, and start paracetamol, two five-hundred milligram tablets, up to four times a day, for the knee.
[SEG0052] person_4 (FAMILY_MEMBER): The other doctor mentioned physio, or a needle into the knee. Which are we doing?

[SEG0053] person_3 (DOCTOR): Not deciding today, and here's my thinking. We might refer you to physio for the stairs and the muscle support. We might do a steroid injection into the knee if the night pain is the bit you want settled faster. If we went for the injection I'd want a plain x-ray of the knee first, but I won't book the x-ray unless we choose the injection.
[SEG0054] person_3 (DOCTOR): Come back in four weeks either way and we'll settle physio or the injection. Ask reception to book that on your way out.

spec.situation: Older patient with knee pain going down stairs and at night; uses diclofenac gel and sometimes tablets from the pharmacy; says no stomach problems and then mentions heartburn; weight discussed; physio or injection discussed, not decided.
features: ambiguous_answer: an answer that sounds like yes but is really 'maybe' ('mm, I suppose', 'sometimes, not really'); recorded with uncertainty or not at all, never as a firm fact.

stopped_or_never_taken: a medicine the patient stopped, was never given or only took once ('I stopped it in March'). Status discontinued, not current; a medicine never taken is not recorded as a medication.

denial_then_admission: the patient first denies a symptom, then later describes it. The label records the symptom as present (the later, fuller answer) and does NOT also record the earlier denial as a negative finding.

third_party_medicine: someone mentions a medicine or condition that belongs to a relative or friend (the sister's biotin, the husband's metformin). It must not appear as the patient's own; a relative's illness can only be family history if said as such.

bad.reason: Heartburn after diclofenac tablets is present, but certainty is not uncertain.
bad.text: heartburn (category=gastrointestinal, status=present, temporality=current, aggravating_factors=after diclofenac tablets, reported_by=patient, certainty=uncertain)

bad.reason: Naproxen 250 mg twice daily for knee is supported, but discontinuation was reported by patient, not full medication details.
bad.text: naproxen (dose=250 mg, frequency=twice a day, indication=knee pain, status=discontinued, reported_by=patient)

omissions.text: Morning stiffness was asked about and was not really present/only sometimes; the doctor explicitly treated it as a 'maybe', not a confirmed symptom.
Swelling was asked about and the patient gave an equivocal answer ('I suppose'); the doctor explicitly treated swelling as a 'maybe', not a confirmed finding.
The patient denied reflux/ulcers initially, but this was later corrected: he does get heartburn after diclofenac tablets, so the earlier 'no stomach problems' was not reliable.
Diclofenac gel adherence detail is missing from the medication entry: he is supposed to apply it twice daily but usually skips the morning dose.
Naproxen discontinuation timing is missing: it was stopped in March.
Glucosamine was specifically discussed and never started, so it should not be on the medication list.
Pulse was measured sitting and 'quite steady'.
The doctor advised to continue diclofenac gel only if the skin tolerates it.
Follow-up detail missing: at the 4-week review they will decide between physiotherapy and steroid injection, and the patient was told to book it with reception on the way out.
